name: Leviticus

overview.author: Traditionally Moses. Over 35 times the book says “The LORD spoke to Moses,” and the New Testament cites its laws as from Moses (e.g., Matthew 8:4).
overview.date: Given at Mount Sinai in the year after the Exodus (about 1445 BC on the early date) and written down during the wilderness period.
overview.audience: Israel’s priests and people camped at Sinai, who needed to know how to worship and live as God’s holy people with His presence in their midst.
overview.setting: Entirely at Mount Sinai, picking up right where Exodus ends with the tabernacle filled with God’s glory.
overview.purpose: To teach Israel how sinful people may approach a holy God through sacrifice and priesthood, and how they should live holy lives in every area: worship, food, health, sexuality, justice, and time.
overview.structure: Sacrifices (1–7), priesthood (8–10), clean and unclean (11–15), the Day of Atonement (16), and the Holiness Code (17–27), with blessings, curses, and vows at the end.

items.title: Ordination of Aaron and his sons
Childbirth, skin disease, and bodily discharges
Atonement for the sanctuary and the people
Holiness in daily life and relationships

themes.title: Holiness
themes.text: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (19:2). Holiness means being set apart for God and reflecting His character.

themes.title: Atonement
themes.text: Sin brings death, but God provides a substitute whose blood makes atonement (17:11).

themes.title: Access to God
themes.text: The tabernacle, priests, and sacrifices show both the wonder and the cost of drawing near to a holy God.

themes.title: Clean and Unclean
themes.text: Everyday laws taught Israel to distinguish life from death and to live with constant awareness of God’s presence.

themes.title: Love of Neighbor
themes.text: The command “love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18) is rooted in Leviticus, alongside care for the poor and the sojourner.

themes.title: Sacred Time
themes.text: Sabbaths, feasts, and the Jubilee shape Israel’s calendar around God’s grace and provision.

keyVerses.quote: Be holy, for I am holy.
For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls.
You shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people.

christInBook.text: The sacrifices point to Christ’s once-for-all offering of Himself (Hebrews 10:1–14).
The Day of Atonement is fulfilled when Jesus enters the true holy place with His own blood (Hebrews 9:11–14).
The scapegoat carrying sins away pictures Christ bearing our sins (Isaiah 53:6; John 1:29).
Aaron’s priesthood foreshadows Jesus, the sinless high priest (Hebrews 7:26–28).
Jesus touches and cleanses lepers rather than being made unclean (Mark 1:40–44).
The feasts find fulfillment in Christ: Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7), Firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), and Pentecost (Acts 2).

crossReferences.note: The priesthood and sacrifices fulfilled in Christ.
“Be holy, for I am holy” applied to Christians.
Jesus declares all foods clean, and the gospel goes to the Gentiles.
Jesus proclaims the year of the Lord’s favor, echoing the Jubilee.

reflection: Leviticus shows that approaching God is costly. How does that deepen your gratitude for Christ’s sacrifice?
God cared about holiness in food, money, sex, work, and rest. Which area of your life most needs to be “set apart” for God?
Jesus bore our sins like the scapegoat. Is there guilt you are still carrying that you need to leave with Him?
Leviticus 19 joins worship of God with care for the poor, the disabled, and the foreigner. How can you practice that this week?
God built rest and celebration into Israel’s calendar. How are you practicing Sabbath rest and joyful remembrance?
Which “clean/unclean” lines in your heart need the cleansing that only Christ gives?

chapterList.title: The Burnt Offering
chapterList.summary: God speaks from the tent of meeting and gives instructions for the burnt offering, a male animal without blemish (from the herd, the flock, or birds for the poor). The worshiper lays a hand on its head and it is accepted to make atonement, and the whole animal is burned as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
questions: What does laying a hand on the animal’s head (1:4) symbolize?
Why did God provide less costly options (birds) for the poor?
How is Christ’s self-offering a “fragrant offering” (Ephesians 5:2)?

chapterList.title: The Grain Offering
chapterList.summary: The grain offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense is a gift of thanksgiving and dedication. A memorial portion is burned, and the rest goes to the priests. No leaven or honey may be burned, and every offering must be seasoned with salt, “the salt of the covenant.”
questions: What might the grain offering represent about dedicating our work and daily bread to God?
Why was salt required with every offering (2:13)?
How does God provide for the priests through this offering?

chapterList.title: The Peace Offering
chapterList.summary: The peace offering, from the herd or flock, celebrates fellowship with God. The fat is burned for the LORD, and the worshiper shares the rest in a meal. The Israelites are forbidden to eat fat or blood.
questions: How does a shared meal picture peace and fellowship with God?
How does Jesus make peace between us and God (Colossians 1:20)?
What does it look like to celebrate your peace with God?

chapterList.title: The Sin Offering
chapterList.summary: The sin (or purification) offering covers unintentional sins, with different requirements for the priest, the whole congregation, a leader, and an ordinary person. Blood is applied to the altar, and the priest makes atonement so they are forgiven.
questions: Why do unintentional sins still require atonement?
Why were the requirements greater for the high priest and the whole community?
How does Hebrews 13:11–12 connect the sin offering to Jesus?

chapterList.title: Sins Requiring a Sin Offering; the Guilt Offering
chapterList.summary: The chapter lists specific cases needing a sin offering (failing to testify, touching uncleanness, rash oaths) and requires confession. It provides a sliding scale down to flour for the very poor. The guilt offering begins for sins against holy things.
questions: Why does God require confession (5:5) along with sacrifice?
What does the provision for the poorest person teach about God’s heart?
How does 1 John 1:9 echo this chapter?

chapterList.title: Guilt Offerings and Priestly Instructions
chapterList.summary: Sins against a neighbor (deceit, robbery, false oaths) are also sins against the LORD and require restitution plus a fifth, then a guilt offering. Instructions follow for the priests: the altar fire must never go out, and rules for the grain and sin offerings.
questions: Why is wronging a neighbor called a breach of faith against the LORD (6:2)?
How does restitution show true repentance? (Compare Zacchaeus, Luke 19:8.)
What does the never-ending altar fire (6:13) suggest?

chapterList.title: More Instructions for Offerings
chapterList.summary: Further instructions cover the guilt offering and the peace offerings (thanksgiving, vow, and freewill), including the priests’ portions. Anyone unclean who eats a peace offering is cut off, and the fat and blood must never be eaten.
questions: Why must the worshiper be clean to share the fellowship meal?
How does Paul warn about eating the Lord’s Supper in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29)?
What are you thankful for that could be your “thanksgiving offering” this week?

chapterList.title: Ordination of Aaron and His Sons
chapterList.summary: Before the whole congregation, Moses washes Aaron and his sons, clothes them, anoints them, and offers sacrifices for their ordination. Blood is placed on their right ear, thumb, and big toe. They remain at the tent for seven days, doing all that the LORD commanded.
questions: Why did the priests need to be cleansed and atoned for before serving?
What does it mean that every believer is now a priest (1 Peter 2:9)?
How does Jesus differ from Aaron as high priest (Hebrews 7:27)?

chapterList.title: The Priests Begin Their Ministry
chapterList.summary: On the eighth day Aaron offers sacrifices for himself and the people, then blesses them. The glory of the LORD appears, and fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the offering. The people shout and fall on their faces.
questions: Why did Aaron need to offer for himself first?
How do the people respond to God’s glory (9:24)? What is a fitting response for us?
What does the fire from God signify about His acceptance?

chapterList.title: Nadab and Abihu
chapterList.summary: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer “unauthorized fire” that God had not commanded, and fire from the LORD consumes them. God says, “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified.” Aaron is silent. Priests are told not to drink before serving and to distinguish holy from common.
questions: Why was God’s judgment on Nadab and Abihu so severe?
What does it mean to treat God as holy in worship?
How can we avoid casual or self-designed worship today?

chapterList.title: Clean and Unclean Animals
chapterList.summary: God lists which land animals, sea creatures, birds, and insects Israel may eat. The chapter closes with the reason: “Be holy, for I am holy.” The food laws set Israel apart from the nations at every meal.
questions: How would these laws remind Israel of their identity every day?
How does Jesus declare all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and why?
What daily habits remind you that you belong to God?

chapterList.title: Purification After Childbirth
chapterList.summary: A mother is ceremonially unclean for a time after giving birth and then brings a burnt offering and sin offering. If she cannot afford a lamb, she may bring two birds.
questions: Why might childbirth involve a period of purification?
How did Mary and Joseph obey this law (Luke 2:22–24), and what does their offering reveal about them?
What does this chapter show about God’s concern for women and families?

chapterList.title: Laws About Skin Diseases
chapterList.summary: Priests examine skin conditions and mold on garments to determine whether a person or item is unclean. A person with a defiling skin disease must live outside the camp and cry, “Unclean, unclean.”
questions: How would it feel to live “outside the camp” (13:46)?
How does Jesus respond to lepers (Mark 1:40–42)?
How is sin like a spreading disease?

chapterList.title: Cleansing from Skin Disease
chapterList.summary: A ritual restores a healed person, using two birds (one killed, one released), washing, shaving, and sacrifices, with blood and oil applied to ear, thumb, and toe. Laws also cover mold in houses.
questions: What might the released bird (14:7) symbolize?
Why did Jesus send healed lepers to show themselves to the priest (Luke 5:14)?
How does Christ restore outsiders to fellowship?

chapterList.title: Bodily Discharges
chapterList.summary: Laws address bodily discharges for men and women, which make a person ceremonially unclean and require washing and offerings. These rules keep Israel from defiling God’s tabernacle in their midst.
questions: What do these laws teach about the seriousness of God’s presence among His people?
How does Jesus respond to the woman with the discharge of blood (Mark 5:25–34)?
How do these laws point to our need for inner cleansing?

chapterList.title: The Day of Atonement
chapterList.summary: Once a year the high priest enters the Most Holy Place with blood to make atonement for himself, the sanctuary, and the people. One goat is sacrificed, and the other, the scapegoat, has Israel’s sins confessed over it and is sent into the wilderness. The day is a solemn Sabbath of rest and self-denial.
questions: Why could the high priest enter only once a year, and only with blood?
What do the two goats together picture about atonement?
How does Hebrews 9:11–14, 24–28 show Jesus fulfilling this day?

chapterList.title: The Place of Sacrifice and the Blood
chapterList.summary: Sacrifices must be brought to the tent of meeting, not offered elsewhere to goat demons. Eating blood is forbidden because “the life of the flesh is in the blood,” given on the altar to make atonement.
questions: Why did God centralize sacrifice at the tabernacle?
What does 17:11 teach about the meaning of blood in atonement?
How does this background help explain Hebrews 9:22?

chapterList.title: Unlawful Sexual Relations
chapterList.summary: God tells Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan. He prohibits incest, adultery, child sacrifice, homosexual acts, and bestiality, warning that such practices defile the land.
questions: Why does God contrast His ways with those of Egypt and Canaan (18:3)?
How does 18:5 (life through obedience) relate to Galatians 3:12?
How can believers honor God’s design for sexuality with both conviction and compassion?

chapterList.title: Holiness in Everyday Life
chapterList.summary: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.” Holiness covers honoring parents, Sabbath, leaving gleanings for the poor, honesty, fair wages, caring for the deaf and blind, impartial justice, and loving your neighbor and the sojourner as yourself.
questions: Why do you think worship laws and social laws are mixed together here?
Who is your “neighbor” and your “sojourner” (19:18, 34)?
Which command in this chapter challenges you most?

chapterList.title: Penalties for Serious Sins
chapterList.summary: God sets penalties for child sacrifice to Molech, consulting mediums, cursing parents, and sexual sins. He reminds Israel that He has separated them from the peoples to be His own.
questions: Why was offering children to Molech so abhorrent to God?
Why does God forbid turning to mediums and spiritists (20:6)?
What does it mean that God has “separated” you to be His (20:26)?

chapterList.title: Holiness of the Priests
chapterList.summary: Priests must avoid defilement from the dead (except close relatives), marry appropriately, and keep their family holy. Descendants of Aaron with physical defects may eat holy food but not serve at the altar.
questions: Why were priests held to a higher standard?
How does Jesus fulfill the requirement of a high priest “without blemish”?
How should spiritual leaders today live (1 Timothy 3:1–7)?

chapterList.title: Holy Things and Acceptable Offerings
chapterList.summary: Priests must not eat holy food while unclean. Offerings must be without blemish to be accepted. The chapter closes: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you.”
questions: Why would offering a blemished animal be an insult to God (see Malachi 1:8)?
What does giving God your best look like for you?
What comfort is there in “I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (22:32)?

chapterList.title: The Feasts of the LORD
chapterList.summary: God sets Israel’s sacred calendar: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Booths. Harvest edges are left for the poor.
questions: What did each feast help Israel remember or celebrate?
How do Passover, Firstfruits, and Pentecost find fulfillment in the New Testament?
How could you build rhythms of remembering God’s works into your year?

chapterList.title: The Lamp, the Bread, and a Blasphemer
chapterList.summary: Pure oil keeps the lamp burning, and twelve loaves are set before the LORD each Sabbath. A man who blasphemes the Name is stoned, and God gives laws of equal justice for both native and sojourner.
questions: What did the twelve loaves represent?
Why does God take blasphemy so seriously?
How does 24:22 show equal justice for all?

chapterList.title: The Sabbath Year and the Jubilee
chapterList.summary: Every seventh year the land rests. Every fiftieth year is a Jubilee: land returns to its original families, and Israelites who sold themselves are freed. “The land is mine,” says God, and the poor are to be helped, not exploited.
questions: What does “the land is mine” (25:23) teach about ownership and stewardship?
How does the Jubilee picture the freedom Jesus announces (Luke 4:18–19)?
How could you trust God’s provision enough to practice generosity and rest?

chapterList.title: Blessings and Curses
chapterList.summary: God promises blessings for obedience (rain, peace, His presence) and escalating discipline for disobedience, ending in exile. Yet if they confess their sin, He will remember His covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
questions: What is the greatest blessing promised in 26:11–12?
Why does God’s discipline increase step by step?
What hope does 26:40–45 offer even after judgment?

chapterList.title: Vows and Dedications
chapterList.summary: Laws cover vows that dedicate people, animals, houses, or land to the LORD, with set values for redeeming them. The tithe of the land and flocks belongs to the LORD.
questions: Why should we be careful about making promises to God? (See Ecclesiastes 5:4–5.)
What does it mean that the tithe is “holy to the LORD”?
What have you dedicated to God, and are you keeping that commitment?

tagline: How a holy God can live among a sinful people
readingPlan: 27 chapters: one chapter a day takes 27 days; two a day takes about 14 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
